Move Fast, Break Things 
Ahead of tariff announcements and presumed negotiations, President Trump said there may 
be “some pain…it will all be worth the price that must be paid” to strengthen the US economy 
(Feb. 2, 2025). However, the outlooks for US equities and factory jobs have different drivers. 
As demonstrated already, protectionist policies will impact markets in 2025. 
US corporates have been key beneficiaries of globalization, deriving product from the 
cheapest sources, selling wherever demand is strongest. US tariffs are an obstacle to this 
efficiency even if US production benefits in the longer-term. 
US tariff increases just ahead remain highly uncertain in scope. To whatever extent they are 
raised, it represents a domestic fiscal tightening in 2025, well ahead of potential tax cuts.  
Either temporary or somewhat more lasting factors have raised US consumer inflation 
expectations, sinking consumer sentiment by 12.6% since December. We would expect 
business confidence measures to follow lower to some extent in coming months. This argued 
for a slight de-risking of our allocations at our latest Global Investment Committee meeting.  
US equities outperformed non-US by 19 percentage points in 2024. In the young 2025, US 
equities are underperforming by around 5 percentage points. EPS expectations for US shares 
will be easily exceeded in 1Q, arguing for a bounce back. However, expected full-year EPS 
gains of more than 10% for the S&P 500 are not as easy to exceed.  
The broadening of profit gains across the world has been consistent with a rise in non-US 
markets in 2025. With all non-US shares just one third of global benchmark allocations, we 
didn’t cut international equities. 
At 22.6X expected EPS for the S&P 500 (vs 14.4X for the rest of the world), we’ve cut our US 
equity weighting 2%, shifting up intermediate US Treasuries. 
A generally rising US trade deficit since 1974 has been associated with a rising value of US 
equities, now twice the market cap of the rest of the world’s shares. Still, we don’t assume US 
and non-US valuations will coalesce.  
We also don’t look to pull large cap US tech shares out of portfolios. US innovation is a 
paramount driver of equity returns and the US’ premium valuation. But one can’t assume an 
absence of innovation or competitive threats from outside the US, particularly after 15 years of 
US outperformance.  
As always, our tactical allocations can react swiftly to add risk during periods of corrections as 
we last did on August 7, 2024 (please see our August 2024 GIC Asset Allocation statement).

Move Fast, Break Things 
The tongue-in-cheek Silicon Valley mantra – move fast, break things – is an ode to innovation that is disruptive at 
times, a willingness to sacrifice for change.  
Innovation is both necessary and usually disruptive for what is left obsolete. Arguably, big parts of most governments 
could use changing. No one believes the US economy is working well for all. In contrast, the US equity market, with an 
annualized return of 14.9% since the Global Financial Crisis, has not been delivering a return worth “breaking” for 
investors.  
The industry drivers of US equity returns can change in time. Yet the world-beating returns of the US equity market 
during the past 15 years have been helped in part by globalization. As FIGURE 1 shows, US equity market valuation has 
risen alongside foreign ownership. The success of US firms in sourcing products globally and selling wherever demand 
is strongest has seen the US market cap share of the world surge as the US trade deficit rose (see FIGURE 2).  
As we described in our last two Investment Strategy Bulletins of February 22 and February 15, US technological 
innovation is the key driver of long-term returns. But the commercialization of this innovation in the US has been aided 
significantly by globalization.

Tariffs are a tax 
Tariffs are paid for by domestic importers. To whatever extent tariffs rise this year, it represents 
fiscal tightening that marginally reduces private after-tax income. This should benefit the US 
Treasury market at the expense of business profits. In time, if production rises in the US to 
provide an equivalent source of supply, the tariff collections will fall or consumers will have 
substituted their demand for another product (please see Investment Strategy Bulletin: When 
the World Divides).  
It is difficult to disentangle the unusual, idiosyncratic impact of issues including the bird flu 
this year from tariff fears (see FIGURE 5). Tariffs on China have barely begun to rise and a host 
of other tariff issues are unsettled. But long-term US consumer inflation expectations have 
risen to a 22-year high this month (see FIGURE 6). Of course, there is scope for this to fall back. 
But the net result has been a drop in US consumer sentiment and a very likely peak for US 
business sentiment (see FIGURES 7-8).

AI Beyond Compute: What We Have Learned From 
DeepSeek 
Compute likely remains a key differentiator in the near to medium term 
DeepSeek’s key breakthrough was its development of a highly cost-efficient algorithm, as opposed to compute, which 
enabled the Chinese tech startup to deliver high-performance training and inferencing on less-advanced AI chips. This 
cost disruption initially raised concerns on the validity of heavy investment in AI infrastructure and drove a sharp derisk 
in semiconductors on January 27th (FIGURE 12). We don’t believe this “AI democratization” means the economy needs 
less compute or chips than before. Lower entry barriers are likely to attract a broader range of players, leading to an 
overall proliferation in compute demand. 
Moreover, rapid evolution in cost and energy efficiency enable greater scale for LLMs, potentially shortening the 
roadmap towards the pinnacle of AI --- Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). According to OpenAI’s five-level framework 
for AI capacity, we’re now at Level 2- Reasoner, where AI is able to exhibit human-level problem-solving skills. 
Prevailing free reasoning models like DeepSeek’s R1 and ChatGPT’s o3mini all belong to this level. We’ve also seen an 
emergence of Level 3 -Agents, where AI systems can take actions on a user’s behalf (FIGURE 13). With the north star of 
AI still out there, investment in the most advanced technology is unlikely to stop anytime soon. Countries like the US 
and China are likely to ramp up state support amid intensified competition. 
Another important implication from DeepSeek is that compute demand is shifting greatly from training to inferencing 
as usage proliferates. Real-time inferencing in advanced AI models (Level 2 and above) consumes much greater 
computational power than the “ChatGPT 3.5” era. The compute demand is also positively correlated to the number of 
active users and queries made on a daily basis. As AI adoptions across industries surge in a short period of time, it 
remains crucial for users to have stable access to mature and integrated AI infrastructure before the next milestone of 
efficiency improvement.  
Indeed, in the latest earnings season, hyperscalers showed no signs of slowing down in AI infrastructure investment. 
Large US tech firms have revised up their capex guidance for 2025 after acknowledging DeepSeek’s breakthroughs 
(FIGURE 14). Collectively, they’re going to invest around 330bn in fiscal year 2025, a 44% growth from last year’s 228bn 
in capex. In addition, initiatives such as the US “Stargate” program is likely to add another 100bn on top of it, though 
the final figures remain uncertain.  
The continued AI infrastructure buildout is likely to support the earnings of leading semiconductors this year, while 
diversified demand in AI compute going forward may yield margin headwinds. We prefer diversification in different semi 
players and see leading equipment makers and foundries hold the widest moats. For hyperscalers that have borne the 
steep costs upfront, their broad client base and established infrastructure will likely start to pay off with increasing 
needs for real-time inferencing and integrated quality AI services on a sustainable basis. We continue to believe in 
certain exposure to the Magnificent 7, but after a 249% gain over the past two years, we believe it makes sense to 
diversify with other risk-reward options as we discuss below

Application layer is the next AI winner 
As we highlighted in January Global Equity Strategy, one clear winner in the era of AI monetization is software and 
internet application companies who are AI users running on light-asset models. Until late last year, software 
companies were struggling to show proven revenue growth as IT budgets were consistently diverted towards expensive 
AI infrastructure. But the application layer has regained momentum lately on the back of DeepSeek’s innovations 
(FIGURE 15). More accessible state-of-the-art LLMs and lower costs to deploy AI indicate a clearer path to 
monetization for application companies, as they now have the flexibility to integrate multiple affordable AI models into 
their existing workflows.  
With more competitors entering the field, the landscape for AI applications in the future may look completely different 
from today. In the near to medium term, large software and internet companies, with their deep R&D budgets and 
established ecosystems, are likely to leverage existing client data and scale solutions more rapidly, realizing margin 
expansion over time. Meanwhile, small- and mid-cap application developers now have a better chance of capturing 
outsized growth if they successfully target niche customer needs. Although trading at a premium to its large cap peers 
already, SMID software is expected to see notable acceleration in earnings this year (FIGURE 16). 
The benefits from wider and more affordable AI models should also broaden into other sectors that are nimble in 
implementing AI to increase productivities, such as healthcare, financial services and consumers.

DeepSeek accelerates the move to Edge AI 
As we mentioned in January Global Equity Strategy, edge AI is emerging as the next critical frontier in AI monetization. 
DeepSeek has essentially accelerated this progress and broadened AI adoption to the mass market for consumers and 
small businesses. With inference efficiency greatly improved, the need for smaller and faster AI chips that could run 
closer to or even within consumer devices could see notable pickup. This could simultaneously drive demand for 
storage, memory and hardware integration in smart phones, PCs and robots.  
Large tech companies with deep expertise, pipeline, and capital capacity have already been experimenting new product 
lines, such as edge AI chips and robots. Diversified revenue streams and in-house AI ecosystems may give them 
flexibility in navigating a highly dynamic environment with AI disruption. Investors could also consider adding exposure 
to smaller chip and consumer equipment makers with niche expertise.  
Renewed growth catalysts for China tech, but caution against 
geopolitical risks 
For the first time in the AI race, innovation is transcending borders and challenging US exceptionalism. DeepSeek’s 
breakthroughs proved the innovative power of open source and international collaborations, which should have 
implications for AI investment.  
The Chinese AI investment story has fundamentally changed in our view, boosting stocks which were largely depressed 
by lagging domestic AI chips and US sanctions on key semiconductors. The fact that China is no longer far behind in the 
AI race and is able to achieve frontier AI capacity without the most advanced GPUs has greatly reignited the investment 
enthusiasm in China tech, which is native to DeepSeek’s technology and has heavyweights in the application layer 
(FIGURE 17). China’s tech and internet sectors have greatly outperformed Nasdaq and broad Chinese market YTD as 
earnings are expected to accelerate in 2025 (FIGURE 18). 
Since DeepSeek, global investors are now reassessing the new possibilities of AI-driven growth in China. Meta’s CEO 
Mark Zuckerberg has commented that the AI competition between the US and China is very close and calls for support 
from US government following DeepSeek’s rapid ascent . Aside from DeepSeek, a few other leading Chinese AI labs also 
have AI models matching international advanced AI capacity. According to a frequently cited independent analysis of AI 
models and benchmark provider Artificial Analysis, as of early 2025, China has 7 advanced LLMs ranked among the top 
20 models globally, closely following the US who has 10 on the list (FIGURE 19). Few other countries have come close so 
far. Another area that has seen China’s progress on the global stage is advanced humanoid robotics.  
Over the first two weeks of February, we’ve seen rapid adoption of DeepSeek’s model across sectors in China, including 
telecom, robotics, EVs and financials. Local chip design is also catching up in inferencing capacity. China is likely to 
leverage the world’s second largest AI talent pool, massive consumer database, efficient high-end manufacturing 
supply chains and integrated internet infrastructure to advance internet and edge AI markets. Unlike the draconian 
regulatory era that abruptly killed the tech bull market in 2021, the Chinese government now backs many of the leading

AI companies given AI’s position in national security. On February 17, it is reported that Chinese President Xi Jinping met 
with prominent leaders of tech and internet companies in China, signaling government’s support to private sectors. 
With that said, risks remain notable as geopolitical tensions between the US and China intensified under Trump 2.0. 
We are likely to see continued US sanctions in the tech space, while tariffs may be less of a concern as most Chinese 
tech companies are largely isolated from international trade. The ongoing deflationary environment and prolonged 
property market malaise domestically could also limit upside.  
Another question for China tech remains whether further scalability and tech innovation could bypass compute and 
hardware bottlenecks amid heightened US sanctions. The DeepSeek innovation was a good start but more needs to be 
done. In any case, we think the shift towards mass market AI adoption alone should warrant some re-rating of China 
tech companies from deeply depressed levels seen prior to DeepSeek in early January. Even after the recent rally, the 
top 7 Chinese tech companies are still trading at a 50% discount to US peers (FIGURE 20). It may be challenging for 
these gaps to fully close anytime soon, but looking into leaders in hyperscaler, software, e-commerce, and edge AI such 
as EVs, consumer equipment, robots, etc. may make sense for suitable investors.

So, China Can Do AI, But Can It Reflate? 
China Outperformed? 
Chinese equities, as measured by the MSCI China index, returned 38% since the start of 2024, outpacing the 25% of 
the US. This outperformance came in three unexpected bursts, the first two were in spring and autumn of 2024, both 
driven by significant packages of policy stimulus. We noted that the policies not only included credit expansion, but 
also capital market reforms that could provide long term benefits. Few investors participated, and many dismissed 
them as in sufficient and incapable of producing sustained earnings growth. And of course, the brief duration of the 
rallies, and the stagnation that followed, caused more tears than joy.  
The most recent one came on the back of the popularity of DeepSeek that instigated a massive re-rating in China tech 
shares. This was augmented by President Xi’s meeting with tech leaders that signaled more policy support for the 
private growth sector. But the origin of the recent rally had nothing to do with government policy. And already, many 
observers are doubting the longevity of this rally. 
In essence, if one stayed out of the Chinese market or thought they could accurately capture the ups and downs of the 
market were taken for a wild ride, not to mention uncertainties over the US-China relationship. But those who believed 
that Chinese leadership and firms can gradually turn around the second largest economy in the world, and therefore 
kept an appropriate allocation, were able to enjoy the extent of this outperformance.  
Going forward, we believe this would still be the case.

Not “Sputnik”! More of a “Taobao” moment 
The emergence of DeepSeek is often dubbed the “Sputnik” moment for AI, drawing a parallel between the US-China 
competition and that between the US and Russia. But this is clearly inaccurate. The more apt comparison is the “Taobao” 
moment, when the world realized that the online marketplace can be free, while platform providers make money from 
smart algorithms.  
Throughout 2023-24, investors were too focused on the breakneck growth of chip designers and other US AI leaders, 
while little attention went to the Chinese side where government policy had brought tech capex down sharply in 2022-
23. But in in 2024, major AI adopters in China (gaming, e-commerce, mobile devices, social media) plowed over $22bn 
into capex, up 40% from the prior year, nearly recovering to the 2021 level, after two years of dramatic decline in capex
(FIGURE 22). The US adopters did not have to suffer the two years of setbacks and went straight to the AI surge with
49% increase in capex in 2024. 
The scale of US investment is also nearly 14x that of the Chinese (FIGURE 22). As a result, it made sense that the initial 
phase of AI competition favored those with bigger wallets who built the infrastructure. But the second phase of 
competition is going to focus on applications and software, the most efficient adopter is likely to capture greater market 
share, not necessarily the one with the most computing power (see Global Equity Bulletin | AI Beyond Compute: What 
We Have Learned From DeepSeek, 18 Feb 2025).  
Chinese adopters have the advantage of lower-cost talent pool, much larger user market, and super platforms that can 
take apps from zero to a billion users in a fraction of the time versus the US. The recent debut of DeepSeek on Tencent’s 
WeChat platform suggests that China’s ecosystem had just begun to exert its influence. Indeed, we have witnessed this 
in the e-commerce and social media industries over the past two decades…after the “Taobao” moment. 
Even after the recent rally, Chinese AI adopters trade at a steep discount, at 18x forward EPS, versus their US 
counterparts, at over 29x. In early 2023, 18 months after “common prosperity” became the main domestic policy stance, 
but before the onset of ChatGPT, the Chinese firms were valued similarly as those in the US on average. Since then, 
Chinese valuations had nearly halved by early 2024 and rebounded in early 2025. But throughout this period, earnings 
growth had been growing strongly from the depressed levels of 2022, outpacing their US counterparts on average. Yet, 
the stock performance had been far inferior due to the country discount.

Can China Reflate? 
While cost efficient AI adoption inject new life into Chinese equities, its macro conditions remain lukewarm. The central 
leadership set a policy priority last September to escape deflation, but progress is limited so far. President Xi’s meeting 
with the tech leaders on February 17 have lifted expectations that more supportive economic measures may emerge 
during the National People’s Congress (NPC) scheduled to start on March 5.  
So far, the macro momentum to escape the two-year-old deflation remains weak. Retail sales growth is recovering 
mildly, but remain below 2021 levels. Manufacturing and fixed investment continue to struggle between growth and 
decline (FIGURE 24). Export growth had been strong last year, but is vulnerable to tariffs. Household and business 
sentiment remain in the doldrums. Consumer inflation had turned slightly positive, but producer pricing remains deeply 
negative, while property prices continue to fall, albeit less severely (FIGURE 25). Developers remain in need of rescue and 
are getting it on a case-by-case basis.  
There are some green shoots, namely credit growth. China’s aggregate financing, a broad measure of credit in the 
economy, made a record at 7.06 trillion yuan in January (FIGURE 26), while the 8.0%y/y growth rate was unchanged 
from December. Non-bank financing took the lead at 9.4%y/y, with government and corporate bond issuance surging 
to a four-year high. New bank loans also made a record 5.13 trillion yuan, but its growth rate remained tepid at 7.2%y/y. 
Still, the January credit growth is notable especially after aggregate new financing shrunk by 3.6tn to 30.3tn yuan in 
2024, suggesting more commitment to reflating the economy with credit support. 
What can be done? Restoring household and business sentiment would go a long way. The past few years of policy 
tightening was not just targeted at the private sector. Employees at state owned enterprises (SOEs) saw their 
compensation and benefits reduced. Hiring dwindled across all white-collar jobs. High paying jobs in the tech and 
financial sectors disappeared, while competition intensified in jobs like logistics. Households have accumulated 17 
trillion yuan of new deposits per year for three years, amounting to some 15% of annual GDP (FIGURE 27). These 
precautionary savings finally began to slow down in 2024, which allowed for a small rebound in consumption. Further 
restoring confidence could potentially mobilize some of these savings.

Portfolio Implications 
In sum, we believe that both AI adoption and policy support are likely to continue to drive Chinese equities back onto 
investors’ radars. We continue to believe in a full allocation to Chinese equities, which amounts to 3% in a global medium 
risk multi-asset class allocation and 13% in an Asia bias allocation.  
Tariffs and geopolitical risks remain on the horizon, but as we noted previously, we believe these risks have actually come 
down in the early days of the Trump administration (see Asia Pacific Strategy | Tariffs Implications for APAC). More 
recently, US efforts to end the war in Ukraine is likely to create another opportunity for China’s foreign policy with Europe. 
We continue to expect potential volatility from US tariff policies, but the threat of higher USD appears limited, as China’s 
recovery takes shape and as China appears not to be in the center of the crosshairs of US tariff policy. We believe the 
PBOC is less likely to use rates and monetary policy to support the economy, while the government is likely to focus on 
debt issuance, as well as regulatory and administrative easing. This backdrop would likely curb potential weakness in the 
Chinese yuan from external trade risks.  
There are risks that short-term bursts of activity may fade, potentially after the NPC. Some investors may be poised to 
take profit, as those who bought in September-October may now be back in the money.  
However, both AI adoption and the path from deflation to inflation are not complete and are both likely to make more 
progress. As we’ve witnessed over the past year, trying to capture brief bursts of market rally can be difficult, but staying 
invested in a gradually recovering market that just had another “Taobao” moment may outperform.
